rows.selection_reason: With zero completed experiments, the highest-priority question is establishing a performance baseline against which all added complexity (multiprofile, learned encoders, image modality, fusion) can be measured. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable configuration in the search space: a standard PCA dimensionality reduction on a single RNA profile with no learned encoder, no image, no aggregation, and no fusion. It serves as the 'null model' floor. Every subsequent experiment—whether it adds a learned RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt), a second profile with aggregation, an image branch, or a multimodal fusion—can be directly compared to this baseline to isolate the marginal contribution of each design choice. Starting with the minimal configuration also avoids confounding multiple design decisions at once and gives the cleanest reference point for the limited experiment budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any predictive signal at all. Before investing in multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or alternative encoders, I need a second unimodal baseline. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest possible comparison: it matches config_001 in simplicity (singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion) and isolates the modality variable. If image accuracy substantially exceeds 48.5%, I know the image channel is the stronger signal and should prioritize image-centric and multimodal configurations. If it is comparable or lower, the problem is intrinsically difficult and I should focus on representation quality (encoder choice) rather than modality or fusion complexity. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about which modality to build upon, making it the highest-information next step under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, establishing RNA as the stronger modality, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is very weak at 20.8%. The key uncertainty is whether moving from a single profile to multiple profiles with aggregation improves the RNA representation. config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the minimal extension of config_001—it changes only the profile setting and adds avgpool aggregation while keeping the same PCA encoder. This cleanly isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it directly builds on our best-performing configuration with a single structural change, (2) the result informs whether multiprofile+aggregation is worth pursuing across all RNA encoders and in multimodal settings, and (3) if it fails to improve over config_001, we can deprioritize the entire multiprofile branch and focus on encoder choice or image improvements instead.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA, multi-profile, PCA, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a strong +0.106 improvement over config_001 (single-profile, 0.485), confirming multi-profile aggregation is highly beneficial for RNA. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), so multimodal fusion is premature. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for multi-profile RNA. This experiment (config_003) tests exactly that—same RNA encoder (PCA n2000), same multi-profile setting, only aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer. It is a clean single-variable comparison that directly extends the best result so far. Establishing the optimal aggregation strategy for RNA before layering on additional modalities or encoders is the highest-information next step under a limited budget, because the aggregation choice will propagate into all subsequent multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the best result so far (acc 0.591, F1 0.573), clearly outperforming singleprofile PCA (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). This establishes multiprofile + avgpool as the strongest profile/aggregation combination. Uncertainty: We have no evidence yet on whether the RNA encoder itself is a bottleneck—PCA is a linear, unsupervised reduction, and a learned representation (scvi) might capture nonlinear structure that matters for classification. Question tested: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable swap of the RNA encoder relative to config_002, isolating the effect of representation quality while holding profile and aggregation at their best-known values. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly answers whether investing in a learned RNA encoder is worthwhile before committing budget to more complex multimodal or scgpt configurations. If scvi improves on PCA, it justifies further encoder exploration; if not, it confirms PCA sufficiency and redirects effort toward multimodal fusion or other design axes. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, and for PCA the same comparison showed avgpool (0.591) clearly outperforming transformer (0.519). However, we have only one data point on aggregation for scvi_n200. Question: Does the avgpool > transformer finding for PCA generalize to the scvi_n200 encoder, or might transformer aggregation extract more from scvi's learned latent representations? This experiment isolates exactly one variable (aggregation: avgpool → transformer) against the current best configuration, making it a clean 1-factor comparison. Why best next step: It is the most direct logical extension of the strongest result, it is low-risk (builds on proven components), and the outcome will either confirm we can rule out transformer aggregation across encoders or reveal a surprising interaction that would redirect the search. Under a limited budget, confirming or refuting this aggregation choice before investing in more complex multimodal or new-encoder experiments is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest single performance lever identified so far (pca_n2000→scvi_n200 in multiprofile/avgpool: 0.591→0.650, ~6 pp). scgpt is the only encoder completely untested. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean one-variable comparison against config_005 (same settings, scvi_n200, acc 0.650), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding profile, aggregation, and modality constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multimodal fusion (where the image signal is very weak at 0.208) or new image encoders, we should first establish the ceiling of the RNA encoder landscape. If scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, it reshapes the entire search strategy; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the best encoder and can confidently build multimodal experiments on top of it. This single experiment reduces the most critical remaining uncertainty about representation quality at minimal cost.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The only image-only result so far (config_010, resnet50 singleprofile) is very weak at 0.208 accuracy, while RNA-only models range from 0.48 to 0.65. We have no data on whether a stronger pretrained image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) provides any meaningful signal for this task. 2) What this tests: config_013 isolates the effect of image encoder quality (ViT-L vs. ResNet50) in the simplest possible setting (singleprofile, image-only), directly answering whether the image modality carries useful discriminative information at all. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: This single-variable test gates an entire branch of the search space. If ViT-L singleprofile remains very weak (<0.30), we can confidently deprioritize all 36 multimodal configurations and redirect limited budget toward refining the RNA pipeline (e.g., confirming scvi_n200 multiprofile as the best RNA setup, or testing scgpt+transformer). If ViT-L shows substantially better performance, multimodal fusion with scvi_n200 becomes a high-value direction. Under a tight budget, this experiment maximizes information gain by resolving the most consequential open question—whether the image modality is worth integrating at all—before committing to any multimodal configuration.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile achieves the best performance (0.650-0.653), while image-only models are near chance (~0.21-0.23), indicating image is a very weak signal. The critical open question is whether fusing this weak image modality with the strong RNA signal can improve upon the 0.653 RNA-only ceiling. This experiment (config_031: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) directly tests that question using the best-known RNA encoder and profile setting. Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because it can learn to downweight the weak image features, making it the more robust fusion strategy when modality strengths are highly asymmetric. If this does not exceed ~0.653, we can confidently conclude image adds no value and focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinement; if it does, we gain evidence that multimodal fusion is worthwhile and should explore further.

Evidence: config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best validation accuracy (0.678) so far, only modestly above the RNA-only scvi_n200 multiprofile avgpool baseline (config_005, 0.650). Image-only models are very weak (~0.21–0.23), so it is unclear how much the image branch is truly contributing versus adding noise. The only multimodal fusion tested so far is 'weighted'; we have no evidence on whether 'concat' fusion would perform comparably or differently. Question: config_030 is identical to config_031 except fusion=concat, giving a clean single-variable A/B test of the fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, isolating one design choice (fusion method) at the current best-performing configuration maximizes information gain. If concat ≈ weighted, the fusion choice is not a bottleneck and we can pivot to testing image encoder quality (ViT-L) or aggregation. If concat is substantially worse, we confirm weighted fusion is critical and should lock it in before exploring other axes. This avoids confounding multiple changes and directly informs whether the modest multimodal gain over RNA-only is robust to fusion design.
